strengths: Addresses a timely and important problem: safety alignment for Large Audio-Language Models (LALMs), an area that is significantly underexplored compared to text-only and vision-language safety.

Provides valuable empirical insights into why vanilla activation steering fails on speech inputs, supported by t-SNE representations showing early and persistent separation of speech activations between safe and harmful queries across layers.

The proposed method, Safe-Ablated Refusal Steering (SARSteer), is conceptually sound, training-free, and computationally lightweight, combining text-derived refusal steering with PCA-based safe-space ablation to mitigate over-refusal.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation covering multiple benchmarks (Figstep-audio, AdvBench-audio, SORRY-Bench-audio, AJailBench), different architectures (Qwen2-Audio, Kimi-Audio, and base models), and specifically designed harmful-safe paired evaluations to track over-refusal.
weaknesses: All audio queries in the newly constructed datasets rely on synthetic OpenAI TTS speech; evaluating or discussing performance on diverse real-world human speech (e.g., varying accents, ambient noise, emotional inflections) would strengthen the practical relevance.

The description of the steering implementation across layers could be clearer: the text notes that steering is conducted per-layer, but does not clarify whether the perturbation is applied across all layers simultaneously or only a subset of intermediate layers, and how the layer-wise hyperparameter was selected.
Lacks an analysis of potential adaptive attacks or robustness against audio-specific adversarial optimization targeting the text-derived steering vector.

strengths: Addresses a timely, critical, and relatively underexplored safety problem: inference-time safety alignment and over-refusal mitigation in Large Audio-Language Models (LALMs).

Provides insightful empirical and representational analysis (e.g., t-SNE analysis across layers in Figure 2), demonstrating why direct adaptation of LLM/LVLM activation steering fails when conditioned on audio inputs due to persistent latent separation.

Proposes a well-motivated and lightweight framework (SARSteer) combining text-derived refusal steering with safe-space ablation via PCA projection, systematically balancing safety enforcement and utility preservation.
Carefully designs paired harmful-safe audio benchmarks using LLM purification and TTS synthesis, allowing for precise measurement of borderline over-refusal via Balanced Refusal Rate (BRR).

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple models (Qwen2-Audio, Kimi-Audio), diverse datasets (Figstep-audio, AdvBench-audio, SORRY-Bench-audio, AJailBench, AirBench), and detailed ablations on hyperparameters (sample size, steering intensity, PCA components).
weaknesses: The audio dataset construction relies exclusively on synthetic speech generated via a single commercial TTS engine (OpenAI TTS-1-HD). It lacks evaluation under diverse acoustic variations, such as different speaker timbres, accents, background noise, or emotional prosody.

The paper lacks comparison against a baseline where the steering vector is derived purely from text (i.e., without audio conditioning in the forward pass of vector extraction). Investigating whether the audio context during vector extraction is strictly necessary would clarify the mechanism.

The algorithmic description lacks explicit detail on layer selection for activation intervention. It appears steering is applied across all layers uniformly, but language model steering literature typically observes layer-dependent sensitivity; clarifying layer-wise intervention details is needed.

The matching-based refusal heuristic in Table 4 relies on common conversational markers (e.g., 'Hello!', 'It is important to note', 'As an', 'I'm an'). These markers can frequently appear in helpful benign responses, potentially introducing noise or false positives into the BRR calculation.

strengths: Timely and important research problem: While safety alignment and jailbreak defenses are heavily researched in LLMs and Vision-Language Models (LVLMs), defense mechanisms tailored to Large Audio-Language Models (LALMs) remain substantially underexplored despite known vulnerabilities to speech inputs.

Insightful empirical diagnosis: The paper offers an empirical analysis (via layer-wise representations and t-SNE) revealing why classical difference-in-means activation steering fails when applied directly to audio inputs due to early representational divergence.

Well-motivated evaluation methodology: Recognizing that standard benign datasets fail to capture borderline over-refusal, the authors construct paired harmful-safe speech datasets (via text purification and TTS) and adopt Balanced Refusal Rate (BRR) to systematically assess safety-utility trade-offs.

Comprehensive empirical validation: Evaluated across two leading open-source LALMs (Qwen2-Audio and Kimi-Audio) across multiple safety benchmarks (Figstep-audio, AdvBench-audio, SORRY-Bench-audio, AJailBench) and general audio capability benchmarks (AirBench), demonstrating consistent reductions in ASR with minimal impact on general utility.
weaknesses: Modest methodological novelty: Conceptually, extracting a refusal direction via text prompts and projecting out the dominant subspace of benign/safe data via PCA/orthogonal projection is closely related to existing representation engineering and concept erasure techniques in the LLM literature (e.g., Arditi et al., 2024; Belrose, 2024). The algorithmic contribution is largely an application of established activation steering principles to the audio-text setting.

Over-reliance on synthetic TTS audio: Both harmful and safe audio datasets are synthesized using OpenAI's TTS service. Natural human speech exhibits rich variability in acoustic features (e.g., emotional tone, pitch, acoustic background noise, regional accents, prosody), which may alter hidden state geometries and challenge the stability of the computed steering vectors.

Lack of adaptive attack evaluation: The evaluation focuses primarily on existing static benchmarks and audio conversions. Because SARSteer applies a fixed, non-input-dependent steering shift during inference, it is crucial to evaluate its robustness against adaptive white-box or gray-box attacks designed to circumvent activation-steering defenses.

Missing operational details regarding layer selection: Algorithm 1 and Equation (2) indicate layer-by-layer intervention, but the manuscript does not adequately clarify whether the steering vector is injected into all layers simultaneously or restricted to intermediate layers, nor does it explore the sensitivity of performance to layer-specific intervention schedules.

strengths: Identifies and thoroughly analyzes a key challenge in multimodal alignment: direct transfer of activation steering from LLMs fails on LALMs due to the substantial latent distributional gap between audio and text representations, supported by both t-SNE visualizations and quantitative CKA measurements.

Proposes a well-motivated and computationally lightweight inference-time defense (SARSteer) combining text-derived refusal steering with PCA-based safe-subspace ablation, providing an effective mechanism to refuse harmful requests without triggering over-refusal on borderline-safe queries.

Comprehensive empirical validation across diverse LALM architectures (e.g., Qwen2-Audio, Kimi-Audio, Voxtral-Mini, Qwen-Omni series) and multiple benchmarks, evaluating safety (ASR), helpfulness (BRR / Safe RR), and general utility (AirBench).

Exemplary supplementary analysis including robustness against adversarial/adaptive attacks (PGD, Gaussian noise, PAIR, GCG), sample-level statistical validation, and human evaluation confirming the reliability and conservative bias of the LLM-as-a-judge protocol.
weaknesses: The majority of the evaluation datasets are constructed by synthesizing text benchmarks via commercial TTS, which may lack some nuances and acoustic diversity (e.g., background noise, varied accents, conversational speech disfluencies) found in real-world spoken interactions, despite initial tests in Appendix B.7.

The method remains data-dependent as it requires an offline calibration set of paired harmful/safe samples to compute the PCA basis and text-derived vectors, though sensitivity analyses show robustness to small sample sizes (n=10-100).

While the theoretical intuition in Appendix A.4 provides a helpful first-order linearization model, it relies on simplifying assumptions regarding the linear separability and orthogonality of the safety subspace in deep non-linear transformer layers.

strengths: Insightful diagnostic analysis: The paper provides a clear empirical explanation (supported by t-SNE visualizations and quantitative CKA measurements) for why direct activation steering fails when naively transferred to audio inputs—specifically demonstrating that harmful and benign speech representations diverge early across model layers, unlike text representations.

Principled and practical framework: SARSteer effectively resolves the audio steering dilemma by deriving refusal directions via text prompt additions while conditioning on the audio, and elegantly mitigates over-refusal on borderline safe inputs by projecting away the safe activation subspace using PCA.

Extensive and rigorous empirical evaluation: The method is validated across five distinct benchmarks (Figstep-audio, SORRY-Bench-audio, AdvBench-audio, AJailBench, AirBench) and across multiple model families (Qwen2-Audio, Kimi-Audio, MiDashengLM, Qwen2.5-Omni, Qwen3-Omni, and Voxtral-Mini).

Thorough supplementary validation: The authors proactively address critical safety and evaluation concerns, including adaptive attacks (PAIR, GCG, PGD), human evaluation of the LLM-as-a-judge protocol (Cohen's kappa = 0.811), statistical variance across seeds, and sample-level projection analysis.
weaknesses: Reliance on white-box model access: Like most activation-steering defenses, SARSteer requires direct access to intermediate hidden activations during generation, rendering it inapplicable to proprietary black-box API endpoints (e.g., GPT-4o audio mode).

Scope limited to speech-to-text generation: The evaluation and formulation are restricted to LALMs that produce textual outputs from audio inputs, leaving open the question of how activation steering transfers to fully end-to-end speech-to-speech models.

Heavy dependence on synthetic TTS datasets: Most safety benchmarks used are synthesized using commercial text-to-speech engines. While Appendix B.7 provides initial tests on acoustic variations from Jailbreak-AudioBench, a deeper investigation into diverse real-world acoustic conditions (e.g., strong background noise, varied room acoustics) would further substantiate real-world robustness.

Specification of intervention layers in the main text: The main text leaves the exact layer-wise application details somewhat implicit (noting layer index is omitted for brevity); explicitly detailing which specific layers are intervened on and whether all layers or intermediate layers yield optimal performance would improve reproducibility.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely, important, and underexplored challenge: safety alignment and defense for Large Audio-Language Models (LALMs) at inference time.

The empirical and representational analysis of why direct LLM activation steering fails in LALMs is insightful. The authors use both t-SNE and quantitative Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) metrics to demonstrate the cross-layer distributional gap between audio activations.

The proposed SARSteer framework is methodologically sound and elegant: utilizing text-derived refusal prompts on the audio query to extract controllable refusal vectors, coupled with PCA-based safe-subspace ablation to suppress over-refusal on borderline-safe queries.

The empirical evaluation is extensive and rigorous, spanning multiple LALM architectures (Qwen2-Audio, Kimi-Audio, MiDashengLM, Qwen-Omni, Voxtral), diverse benchmarks (Figstep, SORRY-Bench, AJailBench, AdvBench), balanced helpfulness metrics (BRR), and general utility benchmarks (AirBench).

The supplementary analysis is exceptionally thorough, providing human validation of the LLM-as-a-judge protocol (Cohen's kappa = 0.811), robustness under audio adversarial perturbations (PGD, Gaussian noise) and adaptive attacks (audio-adapted PAIR and GCG), and multi-seed statistical stability tests.
weaknesses: The evaluation of adaptive attacks, while commendable, primarily tests attacks designed without explicit knowledge of the defense mechanism (e.g., standard audio PGD or text-optimized GCG transferred via TTS). An end-to-end white-box attack specifically designed to optimize audio waveforms to bypass the PCA-ablated steering intervention would provide an even stronger robustness test.

The evaluation of helpfulness and over-refusal relies on keyword matching for the Balanced Refusal Rate (BRR). While standard in the literature and partially supported by the human evaluation in the appendix, string matching can occasionally mischaracterize nuanced conversational responses or non-standard refusals.

The effectiveness of SARSteer varies across model architectures; for example, on Voxtral-Mini-3B in Table 14, SARSteer yields a relatively modest reduction in ASR (from 34.0% to 30.0%), suggesting that model-specific latent geometry can influence the efficacy of linear steering.
